references.text: Isaiah 14:13-15 is the direct Old Testament background to which Jesus alludes. Isaiah describes the king of Babylon as wanting to ascend to heaven but being cast down to Sheol (the realm of the dead). Jesus applies the same imagery to Capernaum: a city that was exalted, yet will be thrust down to the realm of the dead.

Matthew 11:23 is the parallel passage in Matthew's Gospel where Jesus pronounces the same judgment on Capernaum with nearly identical wording: "And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Sheol."
Ezekiel 26:20 uses similar imagery of being cast down to those in the grave and into the depths of the earth, reflecting the theme of being thrown down to Sheol as punishment for pride.

Ezekiel 31:14-16 describes great nations and trees (symbols of powerful empires) being brought down to Sheol, a parallel theme to the judgment on Capernaum, which is cast down from its exalted position.
Ezekiel 32:18 speaks of sinking into the depths of the earth together with those who go down to the grave, sharing the theme of being cast down to Sheol as judgment.

The preceding verse in the context where Jesus says it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for the city that rejects the gospel. This provides the immediate context for the judgment on Capernaum.

Jesus' woes against Chorazin and Bethsaida, which immediately precede the judgment on Capernaum, forming the same series of judgments against Galilean cities that did not repent despite Jesus' mighty works.
Jesus taught in Capernaum early in his ministry, showing that Capernaum had ample opportunity to hear and receive his message, and thus also greater responsibility.

The account of the Tower of Babel, where people attempt to build a tower reaching to heaven, and God intervenes. Pride and self-exaltation met with God's judgment is a recurring theme that also applies to Capernaum.
Job 20:6 describes the wicked one who exalts himself to heaven, yet will still perish, a theme parallel to Capernaum's fate.
Amos 1:4 (and Obadiah 1:4) speaks of the one who exalts themselves and sets their nest among the stars, yet will still be cast down, an image related to Isaiah 14 and Jesus' words about Capernaum.
